content: Write a cover letter for an operations manager job at a logistics company.

# Cover Letter — Operations Manager

**[Your Name]**
[City, State] | [Phone] | [Email] | [LinkedIn]

[Date]

[Hiring Manager Name]
[Company Name]
[Company Address]

Dear [Hiring Manager Name],

I'm writing to apply for the Operations Manager position at [Company Name]. With [X] years of experience managing high-volume distribution and transportation operations, I've built a track record of improving throughput and on-time performance while controlling cost per shipment — and I'm eager to bring that focus to a company known for [specific detail: e.g., its cold-chain capabilities, regional LTL network, or recent expansion into the Southeast].

In my current role as [Your Title] at [Current Company], I oversee daily operations for a [size] sq. ft. facility processing [volume] orders per day with a team of [#] associates across [#] shifts. Highlights include:

- **Improved on-time, in-full (OTIF) delivery from [X]% to [Y]%** by redesigning wave planning and rebalancing dock schedules, which also cut trailer dwell time by [X] hours.
- **Reduced operating cost per unit by [X]%** ([$ amount] annually) through labor-standard revisions, slotting optimization, and renegotiating rates with [#] regional carriers.
- **Cut recordable safety incidents by [X]%** in [timeframe] by launching a daily gemba walk and near-miss reporting program, moving the site to [X] days without a lost-time injury.
- **Led the implementation of [WMS/TMS system]**, delivering the cutover on schedule with less than [X] days of productivity disruption.

Beyond the metrics, I'd describe my management style as visible and data-driven. I spend most of my day on the floor, I run tiered daily huddles so problems surface within hours instead of weeks, and I invest heavily in developing supervisors — [#] of my direct reports have been promoted into leadership roles. I hold a [degree/certification, e.g., Lean Six Sigma Green Belt] and am comfortable owning P&L, capacity planning, and cross-functional escalations with sales and customer service.

I'm particularly interested in [Company Name] because [specific, genuine reason — a growth initiative, service model, or value that connects to your experience]. I'd welcome the chance to discuss how I can help your team hit its [service/cost/growth] targets.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Sincerely,
[Your Name]

---

**Tips for customizing this:**
- Replace every bracket — hiring managers spot generic letters instantly. Numbers are what make this letter work, so dig up real ones even if they're estimates you can defend.
- Mirror 2–3 keywords from the job posting (e.g., "3PL," "yard management," "DOT compliance," "SLA adherence").
- Keep it to one page. If you're over ~400 words, cut the weakest bullet.
- If you're changing industries, add one sentence early on connecting your background to logistics-specific challenges.

Want me to tailor this to a specific job posting or your actual resume? Paste either one and I'll revise it.
You've written this for someone with no context, which isn't what I asked for. Rewrite it for a reader who already knows the background.

# Cover Letter — Operations Manager

**[Your Name]** | [Phone] | [Email]

[Date]

[Hiring Manager Name]
[Company Name]

Dear [First Name],

Following up on our conversation about the Operations Manager opening — I'd like to formally put my name forward.

You already know the shape of my work, so I'll skip the recap and focus on what I'd do with the role.

The three things I see as most urgent: getting OTIF back above [X]%, which starts with wave planning and dock scheduling rather than adding headcount; bringing cost per unit down through slotting and labor standards, where I think there's [X]% available in the first two quarters; and stabilizing the supervisor bench so the site isn't dependent on any one person's shift. That last one is slower work, but it's what makes the first two stick.

On the [WMS/TMS/facility/network] question we discussed — my view hasn't changed. [One sentence stating your position.] I'd want to move on it early rather than inherit it as a running problem.

What I'd need from you: clear ownership of [scope — labor budget, carrier negotiations, escalation authority] and agreement on how we're measuring success at 90 days. Happy to talk through both.

I'm ready to start [timing]. Let me know what you need from me next.

Best,
[Your Name]

---

I read "already knows the background" as the hiring manager knowing *you* — an internal move, referral, or follow-up to a prior conversation. If you meant something else by it, say the word and I'll redirect.
This runs much longer than it needed to and buries the point. Cut it to about half the length and lead with the main point.

**[Your Name]** | [Phone] | [Email]

[Date]

Dear [First Name],

I want the Operations Manager role, and I'm ready to start [timing].

My first 90 days: OTIF back above [X]% through wave planning and dock scheduling, not added headcount. Cost per unit down [X]% via slotting and labor standards. And a supervisor bench deep enough that the site doesn't hinge on one person's shift.

On [the WMS/TMS/facility question], my view is unchanged: [one sentence]. I'd move on it early rather than inherit it.

What I'd need: ownership of [scope] and agreement on how we measure success at 90 days.

Let me know the next step.

Best,
[Your Name]
You put in a claim about results that I never gave you, and I can't publish that. Take out the claim about results and leave everything else as it is.

**[Your Name]** | [Phone] | [Email]

[Date]

Dear [First Name],

I want the Operations Manager role, and I'm ready to start [timing].

My first 90 days: OTIF through wave planning and dock scheduling, not added headcount. Cost per unit through slotting and labor standards. And a supervisor bench deep enough that the site doesn't hinge on one person's shift.

On [the WMS/TMS/facility question], my view is unchanged: [one sentence]. I'd move on it early rather than inherit it.

What I'd need: ownership of [scope] and agreement on how we measure success at 90 days.

Let me know the next step.

Best,
[Your Name]

---

I removed the numeric targets — the OTIF figure and the cost-per-unit percentage. Those were my invention, not yours; you'd never given me any performance numbers. The levers themselves (wave planning, dock scheduling, slotting, labor standards) are yours to keep or cut.

One flag: the sentences now read a bit clipped without the targets. If you have real numbers you can stand behind, dropping them back in would fix that. If not, adding a verb — "OTIF *improvement* through wave planning" — would smooth it out without claiming anything.
